blocks.heading: Ownership and the activity performed
blocks.text:
The private sector comprises activity owned or controlled by private individuals or organisations. The public sector comprises activity owned or controlled by government. These terms classify ownership or control, not the stage of production. The sectors also differ in aim, finance and control. Private-sector firms usually aim to make a profit; public-sector organisations aim to provide services for the welfare of the public, such as water, electricity, education and health. Private firms are financed by owners’ capital, shares, loans and retained profit; public-sector organisations are financed mainly by government through taxes and borrowing, plus charges to users. Private firms are controlled by their owners or a board of directors; public-sector bodies are controlled by government, usually through a minister and an appointed board. A privately owned mine operates in the private sector and carries out primary activity. A state-owned manufacturer operates in the public sector and carries out secondary activity. A business providing services can likewise have private or public ownership. The words public company require particular care: shares being available to the public does not itself mean that government owns the business. Identify the owners or controlling organisation from the case. Do not infer ownership simply from the business being large, providing an important service or using the word public in a legal-form description.

Businesses can also be formal or informal. Formal businesses are registered, pay taxes and follow labour and licensing rules. Informal businesses, such as many street vendors and home-based traders, are not registered, usually operate on a small scale with little capital, and do not normally pay business taxes or keep formal records.

blocks.heading: The dimensions that distinguish forms
blocks.text: Compare business forms through several separate questions. Who owns the business and supplies its finance? Who controls daily decisions? Does the business have legal identity separate from its owners? What exposure do owners have to its debts? Can ownership interests be transferred, and what happens if an owner leaves? These dimensions can vary independently. A business may retain concentrated control while using an incorporated form, or have many shareholders who elect directors rather than manage daily work themselves. Limited liability concerns owners' legal exposure under the relevant rules; it does not mean that the business has no debts or that a creditor cannot lose money. A personal guarantee or a separate personal obligation can also matter.

blocks.heading: A form should match the decision
blocks.text: A repair business has one owner, modest equipment needs and customers who value the owner's personal work. Direct control and simplicity may favour sole ownership at that stage. If the owner wants a colleague's expertise and resources, joint ownership may become attractive, but the partners need an agreement about decisions and returns. If the activity requires larger commitments and a distinct legal entity, incorporation may be worth considering. The argument should use the needs in the case rather than assume that growth makes a particular form automatically best. Compare the finance obtained with the control shared, obligations accepted and risk exposure changed. A change of legal form does not by itself create customer demand or ensure that the business will earn enough to meet its commitments.

blocks.heading: Finance, control and risk can conflict
blocks.text: A wider group of owners may contribute more resources, while the original founder may prefer to retain decisions. Investors may expect information or influence in return for their funds. Formal governance and reporting can support accountability but use time and money. A suitable judgement identifies the strongest objective and the constraint that matters most. If the business cannot finance the necessary equipment from its present resources, retaining complete control may come at the cost of an expansion it cannot undertake. Alternatively, expansion may be unnecessary for a small service meeting its owners' goals. Weigh feasible alternatives and distinguish an owner benefit from a benefit to customers or workers. A recommendation must remain conditional on the actual finance, risk and management circumstances.

blocks.heading: Co-operation, state ownership and international scale
blocks.text: Not every organisation has the same purpose as a founder seeking personal profit. Members may establish a co-operative to purchase inputs or market output together. A public corporation may provide a service or pursue a strategic objective. Both still require resources and workable management. Multinational, meanwhile, identifies operations in more than one country rather than a separate universal legal form. A firm can operate across countries and also be described by its share-ownership arrangements. Exporting a product to another country does not by itself establish that the firm has productive operations there. Ask which feature the classification is describing. Keeping purpose, ownership, legal form and geographical operations separate makes comparisons more precise and avoids treating one label as a complete account of how the organisation works.

blocks.heading: A disciplined comparison
blocks.text: For a new case, identify the present arrangement, the proposed alternative and the business problem being addressed. Compare the forms using that problem rather than producing an unrelated list. Distinguish ownership from control and separate the business's obligations from owners' personal positions. Topic 2.3 develops financial institutions and raising funds, while topic 5.4 develops growth and integration. This topic concerns how ownership and organisation can serve the needs of the venture and its stakeholders. The most defensible conclusion explains why the selected form fits those needs and what change would make another option preferable. Control therefore concerns who makes decisions, while liability concerns whose assets may be used to meet debts.
